				<docs>http://blogs.law.harvard.edu/tech/rss</docs><item><title> The geography of financial frictions</title><description>This paper studies the aggregate implications of the geography of financial frictions faced by firms in Europe. Using proprietary data from the European Central Bank’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises, we document substantial regional heterogeneity in the access to external finance, which is persistent over time and matters for monetary policy: high-friction countries are less responsive to monetary shocks. We formalize these findings in a tractable New Keynesian model of a monetary union with 22 countries that are heterogeneous in financial frictions (loan recovery rate), productivity, and size. High-friction countries respond less to monetary shocks because firms face a steeper marginal cost curve and a lower capital elasticity. This result is robust to firm heterogeneity with endogenous default, liquidity constraints, and capital mobility. Financial frictions shape the output-inflation trade-off across space: in high-friction countries the same output gain costs more inflation. Convergence experiments show that financial integration in the spirit of a European Savings and Investments Union trades off the effectiveness of monetary policy against financial stability.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3312~6f0e0bfceb.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3312~6f0e0bfceb.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> Monetary policy, segmented capital markets and innovation</title><description>We identify a novel mechanism linking monetary policy, innovation, and capital-market segmentation. When capital markets are imperfectly integrated, contractionary monetary policy tightens the financing constraints of externally financed firms, amplifying the decline in innovation induced by tighter financial conditions; monetary easing operates in reverse. Using granular euro-area firm-level data on balance sheets and patenting, matched with bank-level and credit-registry information, we show that monetary policy affects innovation through financing constraints. The effects are strongest for firms with high intangible intensity and for firms operating in AI-related sectors. Financing structure is central: firms that rely heavily on bank credit experience larger declines in patenting following monetary tightening, whereas firms with diversified access to external finance, particularly equity, are substantially less affected. Capital-market segmentation thus amplifies and prolongs the effects of monetary policy on innovation. Greater financial integration can broaden firms’ financing options, reduce their reliance on bank credit, and thereby attenuate this amplification mechanism.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3311~66cc2a4d65.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3311~66cc2a4d65.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Tue, 17 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> The macroeconomic effects of defence spending: what impact beyond GDP?</title><description>This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for a panel of up to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025 using Panel Local Projections. We look beyond the output multiplier that dominates the literature to trace the price implications of defence spending and the demand-side channels through which effects operate. A key methodological contribution is a country-specific order-date adjustment for capital expenditure, constructed from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, which shifts the estimated (unitary) peak GDP multiplier from around year one to approximately year three to four. Under this specification, the HICP inflation response is higher and occurs earlier. Capital expenditure drives the positive output effects, whereas personnel and intermediate consumption generate stronger inflationary pressures per unit of fiscal impulse. Capital spending induces additional recurrent costs, standing at about 30 cents per euro spent over five years. Multipliers are also found to be substantially lower, on average, in high public debt regimes.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3310~6ef5699d9a.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3310~6ef5699d9a.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Thu, 12 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> The real and financial effects of local corporate tax increases: evidence from linked firm–bank data</title><description>We study how local corporate tax increases affect firms’ financing and real activity. In Portugal, municipalities independently set a surtax on corporate income, generating plausibly exogenous variation across space and time. We link the universe of corporate balance sheets and profit-and-loss statements to loan-level data from the Bank of Portugal’s credit registry, allowing us to track firms’ liquidity, leverage, borrowing costs, and credit quality alongside revenues, employment, and productivity. We estimate local-projection difference-in-differences models that address staggered treatment timing and dynamic responses. Surtax hikes immediately tighten financing conditions: liquidity falls, implicit interest rates rise, debt increases at shorter maturities, and non-performing loans become more prevalent. These strains spill over into real outcomes: firms reduce sales and employment and experience persistent declines in total factor productivity. Effects are strongest among small firms, where leverage rises in response to liquidity losses. We also find higher exit and relocation probabilities, but no gains in neighboring output, pointing to inefficient reallocation. Our results highlight how local tax policy can transmit through both financial and real margins, with implications for fiscal design in decentralized settings.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3309~4e8af93b3a.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3309~4e8af93b3a.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> Unlocking supervisory effectiveness in credit risk: insights from the ECB’s supervisory findings and measures</title><description>This paper provides an assessment of supervisory effectiveness in credit risk using confidential data from ECB Banking Supervision. The analysis covers 8,106 supervisory measures issued and closed between 2016 and 2025. A central contribution is the construction of a measure level indicator of supervisory effectiveness based on large language model (LLM) analysis of supervisory narratives and closure justifications. The indicator captures whether supervisory measures resulted in full remediation of the underlying deficiencies. Using logistic and duration models, we examine the characteristics of findings, measures, and banks associated with remediation outcomes and remediation speed. The results show that multi-faceted findings are a key driver of supervisory outcomes. Measures related to data, reporting, and IT deficiencies are less likely to achieve full remediation and require longer remediation periods. Measures originating from on-site inspections are associated with higher remediation rates and faster closure. Stronger governance is also associated with more successful remediation outcomes.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3308~a6e82e37aa.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3308~a6e82e37aa.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> Deep-π*: a neural network estimate of trend inflation</title><description>Most empirical models of trend inflation treat it as a latent random walk driven by unobserved shocks, so they cannot say which economic conditions move it. Deep- π*makes the innovations to the trend a possibly nonlinear function of a large number of macroeconomic indicators, estimated with neural networks, so that Shapley values can be used to attribute every movement of the trend to the indicators behind it. Two complementary loss functions define a current trend, which fits inflation today, and a forward-looking trend, which best predicts inflation over the next year. In US data, employment-related variables were the largest contributors to the post-pandemic rise of the current trend. However, the forwardlooking trend rose earlier, with real activity, employment, and money and credit as the main drivers from the start of the pandemic, and peaked eight to twelve months before the current trend. Both trends looked through most of the movements in energy and commodity prices. The contributions of the indicators are nonlinear, with sizeable interactions between them. Re-estimated every month during the surge, the model forecast inflation more accurately than the standard UC-SV model and a random walk, and in early 2021, when professional forecasters expected inflation of 3% or less, the forward-looking trend was already signalling an increase in persistent inflation.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3307~d3d2e0c5e4.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3307~d3d2e0c5e4.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> Debt maturity and government spending multipliers</title><description>Government spending effectiveness depends critically on how it is financed. Using state dependent SVAR models and local projections on post-war US data, we show that fiscal expansions financed with short-term debt generate significantly larger output multipliers than those financed with long-term debt. This difference mainly stems from private consumption responses: short-term financing crowds in consumption while long-term financing does not. Torationalize this finding, we construct an incomplete markets model in which households invest in short-term and long-term assets. Short assets provide liquidity/safety services; households can (more readily) use them to cover sudden idiosyncratic spending needs. An increase in the supply of these assets, through a short-term debt-financed government expenditure shock, boosts private consumption. We first show this mechanism analytically in a simplified model, and then quantify it in a carefully calibrated New Keynesian model. We find that fiscal multipliers differ substantially across financing modes, with short-term-financed shocks typically exceeding unity while long-term-financed shocks typically fall below unity. We show these differences persist across monetary and fiscal policy regimes, with important implications for optimal debt management and stimulus design.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3306~028a82bc67.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3306~028a82bc67.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> Elastic in cash, inelastic in repo: hedge funds in the treasury and repo markets</title><description>The functioning of sovereign bond markets is closely intertwined with repo markets, where investors finance long positions and source bonds for short sales. We show, theoretically and empirically, how conditions in the cash bond market fundamentally shape repo rates: When demand for cash bonds exceeds available supply, arbitrageurs, notably hedge funds, step in to bridge the gap by shorting bonds and borrowing them in the repo market. These arbitrage strategies drive a wedge between monetary policy rates and repo rates, generating “specialness”. To investigate the drivers of investors’ demand for repo contracts, we obtain regulatory data covering the entire universe of repos backed by German sovereign bonds. We identify the ultimate borrowers and lenders of securities and estimate their demand and supply elasticities for the repo market. Supply, dominated by the public sector, accounts for 87% of the aggregate elasticity. Demand, driven mainly by hedge funds, is strongly inelastic: a 10% increase in borrowing costs reduces their borrowing by only 1%. Despite being among the most price-elastic investors in cash bond markets, hedge funds are inelastic in repo markets because their bond borrowing bridges the preferred-habitat demand in the cash bond market: their elasticity is inherited from their cash-market counterparties rather than being a primitive. As a result, repo rate specialness emerges as the equilibrium price reflecting demand pressures in the cash bond market, of which collateral scarcity from central bank purchases is a special case. Consequently, the same cash bond market imbalances affect both the pricing of safe assets and repos, two markets that are of crucial importance for the transmission of monetary policy.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3305~877e68c2b7.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3305~877e68c2b7.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> ECB perception of non-banks: a machine learning-based approach</title><description>This paper studies the European Central Bank’s (ECB) perception of non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) and how this perception is publicly communicated. We construct a perception index based on ECB speeches over the period 1998–2025. Sentiment in references to non-banks is classified by a large language model that we fine-tune on our own hand-labeled dataset constructed for this purpose. The resulting index reveals a predominantly negative and declining perception over time, particularly since the Global Financial Crisis. Negative sentiment is primarily associated with concerns related to financial stability and regulatory needs, whereas positive sentiment reflects the role of non-banks in fostering financial innovation and supporting market functioning. The index is made publicly available for future research.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3304~9082a5f181.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3304~9082a5f181.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 12:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> The effects of geopolitical risk on sovereign debt holders in the euro area</title><description>We use confidential granular data on euro area sovereign bond holdings to examine the heterogeneous behavior of investor types in response to country-specific geopolitical risk shocks. By distinguishing investor categories and accounting for their bond holding dynamics over time, we provide an empirical assessment of how different bond holders react to geopolitics. The analysis employs country-level geopolitical risk indices of the country of sovereign bonds, and applies local projection methods to estimate the dynamic responses of various investor groups to geopolitical risk shocks. In the case of high-debt euro area countries, i.e. Italy, France, Spain, and Belgium, we examine how geopolitical risks may trigger shifts in investor behavior that, in turn, could pose risks to fiscal sustainability.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3303~10146acd61.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3303~10146acd61.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0100</pubDate></item><item><title> Headwind or tailwind? How banks interpret borrowers’ AI exposure</title><description>General-purpose technologies create large opportunities but make their distribution across firms difficult to assess in real time. We use banks as interpreters of the rise of generative AI by studying lender-specific probability-of-default (PD) estimates for private firms in four large euro-area economies. As public attention to AI rises after ChatGPT, banks lower assessed default risk for borrowers in highly AI-exposed industries by about 5%. The reassessment is weaker for labor-intensive firms and stronger among lenders with pre-existing industry expertise. Yet the favorable industry-level effect is accompanied by a systematic reordering within product markets: banks reassess firms with stronger pre-ChatGPT market positions less favorably relative to their competitors, compressing the risk advantage associated with market leadership. Credit allocation moves in the same direction, with market leaders experiencing relatively lower drawn and committed credit, more relationship exits, and fewer new lenders. The reordering also predicts subsequent bad-credit events beyond banks’ consensus PDs. Internal bank assessments therefore provide a forward-looking measure of how generative AI is expected to reshape competitive risk.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3302~7ff8a286bc.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3302~7ff8a286bc.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate></item><item><title> Stop believing in haircuts - at least the way you think about them</title><description>We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level supervisory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirement, we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down. In funding-driven trades, the leverage constraint has no effect, higher convenience yields raise haircuts through the rehypothecation channel, and broader client outside options lower them. We rationalise these patterns in a bilateral bargaining model with periodic haircut renegotiation. Consistent with the model, constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility and weaker pass-through of ECB policy rate changes in the collateral-driven segment. Post-crisis bank regulation thus carries potential unintended consequences for repo market functioning and the transmission of monetary policy.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3301~1585c96063.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3301~1585c96063.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate></item><item><title> When less is more: behavioral effects of CBDC holding limits</title><description>Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3300~0277bae3af.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3300~0277bae3af.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate></item><item><title> The heterogeneous bank lending channel of monetary policy</title><description>How does heterogeneity in banks’ interest-rate risk exposure shape monetary policy transmission? We develop a quantitative macroeconomic model of heterogeneous banks to answer this question. We establish an irrelevance result: differences in interest-rate risk exposure between fixed- and variable-rate banking systems matter for transmission only when bank solvency concerns become relevant. Calibrating the model to the euro area, we show that idiosyncratic default risk pushes a substantial share of banks toward the solvency threshold, making heterogeneity quantitatively important. When policy rates rise, fixed-rate banks suffer net interest margin compression—funding costs increase while legacy loan income stays unchanged—eroding capital and triggering sharper deleveraging. The lending elasticity to monetary policy is one-third larger in fixed-rate economies. The effects extend to financial stability: tightening raises bank failure rates in fixed-rate systems while lowering them in variable-rate systems. The results provide a rationale for macroprudential and monetary policy coordination and for monetary policy gradualism.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3299~01776adb36.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3299~01776adb36.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate></item><item><title> What analysts hear and why it matters for monetary policy</title><description>We introduce a novel measure of how European Central Bank (ECB) monetary policy is interpreted by analysts at major investment banks. We construct a “policy interpretation shock” based on the language used in analysts’ reports covering monetary policy decisions by the ECB’s Governing Council (GovC). The main identifying assumption is that changes in the way analysts report on policy communication by the GovC—that is, the change in the policy tone from the preview report to the recap report—reflect unexpected information revealed by the policy event. Using GPT-based sentiment extraction, we show that the tone in these reports closely tracks that of the GovC, often even anticipating shifts in tone. Changes in the policy tone before and after meetings capture how market intermediaries interpret and adjust their assessment of policy decisions. These interpretation shocks are followed by contractionary macroeconomic responses and systematic movements in financial-market prices. These findings underscore the important role of communication in shaping expectations and influencing economic outcomes.</description><link>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3298~06485c09a7.en.pdf</link><guid>https://www.ecb.europa.eu//pub/pdf/scpwps/ecb.wp3298~06485c09a7.en.pdf</guid><pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200</pubDate></item></channel></rss>
